articles.title: Claude Code found my app’s shared contract in two MCP calls. Then the records ran out.
articles.text:
Claude Code found my app’s shared contract in two MCP calls. Then the records ran out.
Every Claude Code user has watched a new session start from zero. You open it on a system you built last week, ask for a small feature, and the agent begins by rediscovering your own architecture: which service owns the data, which frontend calls it, which type the two of them share. The conversation that explained all of that is gone or compressed into a summary, and the source files show what exists without saying what depends on what.
So far, the main answer is memory. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md instructions and its own auto-memory notes at the start of every session, and since September 17, the redesigned Projects, in beta in Claude Code cloud sessions, keep a shared memory across threads, so Claude can recall that “the release moved to Friday” or “who to check in with before touching the billing service.” I wanted to test a different source of context: the dependency records a build platform writes when it creates each version of a component.
Disclosure: I’m an engineer at Bit Cloud, a platform that builds, hosts, and deploys even a single app from its first component, with coding agents working on it over MCP. I asked Claude to build on it to see what an agent can do when the platform records each part and its dependencies as they are versioned. The project and its build records are public.
What can a fresh session recover without memory?
The system was a small support console I had built with Claude Code earlier, and I wrote up how I built and deployed it separately. The prompt that started that build mentioned tooling in two words, “using Bit”, and otherwise described the product. It has four components: a React app, an Express service backed by MongoDB, a shared ticket entity, and a platform component that puts the app and the service behind one gateway. All four are versioned in a public scope, bit-oss.support, and the console runs in production over HTTPS.
To test what the records alone could carry, I opened a fresh Claude Code session in an empty workspace, with no conversation history and no local code, and asked:
Add filtering by ticket status and assignee to the support console in bit-oss.support.
Claude checked the workspace and found no local components. Its next message was: “The workspace is empty, so the support console lives remotely. Let me read the bit-oss.support scope through the MCP.” It called `read_scope` for `bit-oss.support`. That returned the four components and their dependencies. It then called `read_components` for the app, service, and ticket entity, retrieving API references and file inventories before importing source or editing code.
The app and service both depended on the same version of the ticket entity. Its class documentation read, “shared between the support service and the agent-facing app,” and the API reference included that sentence. The project could supply this context without the original conversation.
Claude imported all four components with `bit import`, inspected the source, and implemented client-side filtering within the app. Validation reported 41 passing tests, including nine new filtering tests. MCP helped it discover the system; source inspection and tests established how to change it. The change stayed inside the app, leaving the shared ticket entity and the service alone. Knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch.
Where did the records run out?
They ran out at behavior. The app’s API reference does list the routes it calls, `GET /tickets`, `POST /tickets`, `PATCH /tickets/:id` and `POST /tickets/:id/comments`, in the documentation for a fake service it uses in tests, but nothing checks that list against the real service. The records told Claude which components shared the ticket contract; whether the routes on each side still matched had to be read by hand and tested.
A green build also proves less than it seems to. The MongoDB integration tests skip when their temporary database cannot start on the CI runner, so a passing build doesn’t show they ran. I checked persistence by hand: create a ticket, add a comment, restart the platform against the same database, and see that both are still there.
And this is a demo, with a predefined demo account and a public signing secret. Concurrency control, migrations, recovery procedures, and mandatory database tests are all still to do. That is ordinary engineering work, and it is where I want an engineer’s time to go.
Memory files or dependency records?
Memory holds what someone chose to write down. In Claude Code, that means CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md) instructions a person writes, and auto-memory notes Claude writes from corrections and preferences, and the redesigned Projects add decisions, such as why an export was dropped, which no build system will ever record. Each note is accurate as of the moment it was written. Claude Code records each memory file’s write time, and its documentation explains why: “the timestamp shows how current the fact is.”
The build system writes a dependency record when it creates a component version, and it is part of that version. When the support app was versioned, the build system recorded its dependency on one specific version of the ticket entity, without anyone deciding it was worth noting, and the record cannot drift from the version it describes. And because `read_scope` returns each component at its latest version, the records Claude read were current. A memory note carries the time it was written, but nothing ties it to a code version. In the test, the session had no conversation and no local code. The only memory in the workspace was the generic AGENTS.md that `bit new` writes, which tells the agent to look things up on the platform, and the records did the rest: they were enough to find the shared contract.
The two cover different ground and work best together: memory for intent, such as the release date, the person to ask, or why a feature was cut, and records for structure and meaning, which version of what depends on which. Nx serves its project graph to agents over MCP, and Sourcegraph serves code search and navigation across repositories; both do that well. For this test, I wanted something narrower: a record per component, written when its version was created, that still holds when the other side of a dependency lives somewhere the agent hasn’t indexed.
When should a team start?
At the first component. The records in this test cost nothing extra, because they were written as each version was made, starting on day one. I had created the workspace with `bit new`, which supplied the Bit Cloud MCP connection in `.mcp.json` and an AGENTS.md with instructions for the agent, and at the start of the original build Claude used that connection to look through an existing design-system scope for parts it could reuse; the four components now depend on 16 that already existed, ten of them from that design system. Rebuilding that map later, after one team renames a shared field and another finds out from its error logs, is the expensive version of the same work.
None of it requires our product; it just needs dependencies recorded wherever the work happens.
Agents can already reach production, and what they still lack, on every request after the first, is a view of the system they are about to change. That view is cheapest to build before the second component exists.

articles.title: Porsche officialise la Mission S : tout savoir sur la remplaçante de la 918 Spyder qui s'apprête à débarquer
articles.text:
« S » comme « Super bien » ? Plutôt « S » comme « Supercar », voyons ! Porsche a en effet validé le nom de sa nouvelle bombe qui remplacera les iconiques Carrera GT et 918 Spyder. La Mission S, qui sera officiellement révélée le 15 octobre, ne devra pas se louper pour redresser la barre. S’il ne s’agira aucunement d’un modèle de conquête, l’auto impactera lourdement l’avenir de la marque avec une direction artistique inédite.
Entendez par là qu’elle inaugurera la nouvelle orientation stylistique de Porsche sur une plateforme inédite de la tête aux pieds. C’est ce qu’a confirmé Michael Leiters, le PDG de la marque, dans un entretien accordé à Auto Express : « nous développons une plateforme pour supercar et nous comptons l’utiliser comme base pour une nouvelle voiture de sport à moteur central, nettement supérieure à la 911 ».
Le pari de l’hybride rechargeable : pourquoi Porsche a changé d’avis
Cette annonce confirme les grandes prétentions de ce nouveau modèle, qui se placera au sommet de la gamme. Aucune information n’a cependant encore été donnée à son sujet. Mais s’agissant d’un véhicule avec un moteur en position centrale, il est probable, sinon obligé, que ce soit un hybride rechargeable hautes performances. Traduction : les machines électriques serviront surtout à doper le bloc essence au détriment de l’autonomie électrique.
C’est donc une contradiction majeure avec le concept Mission X présenté en 2023 qui se targuait d’une mécanique exclusivement électrique. Les plans semblent donc avoir changé entre temps. Compréhensible : face à une demande en modèles haut de gamme à batterie plus qu’incertaine, Porsche préfère jouer la sécurité, surtout que la marque n’est pas au plus haut de sa forme après une année 2025 particulièrement difficile.
1 000 ch pour redresser la barre : rendez-vous le 15 octobre
Rappelons en effet que les droits de douane américains doublés d’un ralentissement notable des ventes sur le marché chinois n’ont pas arrangé les comptes de Stuttgart. Un risque considérable a en parallèle été pris avec la fin de production des Macan et 718, qui composaient pourtant l’entrée de gamme de Porsche. Le SUV ne sera remplacé qu’en 2028 alors que le coupé, lui, se convertira uniquement à l’énergie électrique dès l’année prochaine.
La Mission S devra donc assurer l’actualité du constructeur pendant quelques mois. Pour attirer toutes les attentions, elle devrait ainsi reprendre le style du sensationnel concept Mission X. Une allure extrêmement racée est donc attendue avec des lignes ultra fluides singeant sans retenue les voitures de compétition. La puissance de l’ensemble pourrait atteindre les 1 000 ch.

articles.title: AMD EPYC 8005 SKU List and Value Analysis: Mainstream Sorano's Big Stride
articles.text:
A few months back AMD launched their EPYC 8005 “Sorano” family of server chips. The mainstream server counterpart to AMD’s high-end EPYC 9005 chips, Sorano filled a significant hole in AMD’s chip lineup by bringing their Zen 5 architecture to a more modest server platform.
As we noted in our review at the time of the launch, Sorano has become a rather significant offering for AMD not only because of the market it fills, but because of just how much it has improved over its own predecessor, the Zen 4-based EPYC 8004 Siena. With a larger number of cores, far higher clockspeeds, and support for much faster DDR5 memory, Sorano made AMD’s SP6 platform a far more capable and competitive offering in the market.
A consequence of that, however, is that almost everything that customers knew about the 8000 series went out the window; despite using the same socket, the Sorano chip family is significantly different in terms of everything from performance and price to the number of individual SKUs within the chip stack. So what are the highlights among the EPYC 8005 family, and what chips should customers go with? To answer that, here is ServeTheHome’s look at the EPYC 8005 product stack, outlining what some of the best options for different scenarios/optimization points.
AMD EPYC 8005 SKU List and Value Analysis
First up, here is the complete list of EPYC 8005 chip SKUs.
For their first generation of 8000 series parts, the EPYC 8004 Siena, AMD kept things relatively simple with a modest product stack and consistent features among all of the chips, and that is once again the case for Sorano. The mid-tier, single-socket server platform does not gate any features behind specific SKUs, and as a result every chip from the entry-level 8 core 8025P to the top-end 8635P gets access to same set of features. This includes 6 channels of DDR5 memory support (including 2DPC support), 96 PCIe Gen5 lanes, and, of course, AMD’s Zen 5 CPU architecture. With Sorano being a notable step up here since these are AMD’s higher-clocking full-size Zen 5 cores, and not the compact cores used in Siena.
For potential customers, this simplifies the calculus behind picking which chip to go with by quite a bit. The only real decisions to be made are around core counts, power consumption, and all of the second-order effects thereof. Drop-in upgrades are even a viable option here since AMD is using the same SP6 socket as with the EPYC 8004 generation – though as we have seen, some vendors are releasing new motherboards for Sorano anyhow.
Even with just 7 chip SKUs, however, the spread between them in core count, clockspeeds, and power consumption are significant. The SP6 IOD can be connected to up to 12 Zen 5 CCDs, so AMD has run the gamut here, with between 8 and 84 CPU cores. This means that while they all share the same platform and architecture, the resulting performance of these chips can be quite different depending on the workload. All of which makes understanding and profiling a target workload all the more important in choosing a chip.
One important factor is going to be how well a workload scales up over multiple cores, versus requiring faster individual cores to hit its best performance. Every single chip SKU has a maximum single core turbo clockspeed of 4.5GHz (a significant improvement from EPYC 8004), so very lightly threaded workloads have a lot of headroom. But, generally speaking, one is not buying an EPYC CPU just to run a couple of threads. Rather, there is some major scale needed here in terms of core counts, I/O lanes, memory bandwidth – or possibly all three.
Taking a look at all-core turbo clockspeeds, we see that clockspeeds here are almost, but not entirely, inverted with core counts. The 84 core EPYC 8635P offers an all-core turbo boost speed of just 3.45GHz, while the 24 core 8225P hit 4.1GHz, and the smallest 8025P can go higher still. The outlier that breaks this pattern is the 16 core 8125P, which despite having fewer cores than the 8225P actually has a lower all core turbo clockspeed.
Outside of the 8125P, no single chip here is quite the sweet spot for per-core performance. But the middle-child 8325P has the strongest claim.
Shifting over to power consumption, AMD’s default TDPs are directly proportional to the core counts, even with the lower core chips offering higher average clockspeeds. For “performance at all costs” there is the 8635P with its 84 cores and 225 Watt TDP. With 20 more cores than the next-fastest chip it is the clear winner in terms of throughput. And, somewhat surprisingly, it is a lot more power efficient than the next chip down as well; the cost of going from a 64 core chip to an 84 core chip is just 15 Watts at default TDPs. AMD’s default TDPs vary from chip to chip, but in general the higher-end Sorano chips are all relatively close to each other in TDP at around 200 Watts – thanks in part to those higher clockspeeds we talked about earlier.
This also means that there is a clear and consistent progression from one part to the next in regards to how much power is needed per core – and really, the overall energy efficiency of the chip. The top-end 8635P ends up being the most efficient, at just 2.7 Watts per CPU core. This rises to a bit over 4.1W with the 48 core part, and finally to nearly 12W per core with the 8 core 8025P. With the entire EPYC 8005 family sharing the same IOD with the same memory and PCIe support, this is a classic case of where the power costs of the uncore (or IOD, in this case) are getting amortized over fewer and fewer CPU cores as the overall core counts drop down.
The flip side to that general decline in per-core energy efficiency is that fewer cores to amortize the impact of the IOD also means that there are fewer cores sharing/competing for other uncore resources, which can be beneficial in other ways. A prime example is the amount of L3 cache per core, which generally increases as the CPU core counts decrease. This is chiefly due to how AMD goes about building these SKUs and the number of CCDs they use, with most SKUs utilizing CCDs with multiple disabled cores – leaving more cache for the rest of the cores.
With 384MB of L3 cache, the top-end 8635P is, of course, the most cache-filled chip. But with so many cores, it also works out to be tighter on cache per core than most, at just under 4.6MB per core. Though it is the 64 core 8535P that is actually the most cache-contested chip here, at just 4MB per core thanks to AMD using 8 fully-enabled CCDs. Fittingly, the smaller core count chips have the most cache per core overall; the 8435P and 8225P both have 5.3MB per core, while the remaining three SKUs all get a spacious 8MB of cache per core.
Especially with AMD not producing 3D V-Cache server part in this generation, this makes the 8325P and its ilk one of the best options for highly-threaded workloads that strongly benefit from additional L3 cache.
As for overall memory bandwidth, with all seven 8005 chip SKUs sharing the same 6 channel DDR5-6400 memory controller, the amount of memory bandwidth on the SP6 platform is fixed. Or to put it another way, the amount of bandwidth per core is directly (and inversely) proportional to the core count. With 307GB/second of memory bandwidth overall for the platform, the 8 cores on the 8025P get an ample 38GB/second each; while at the top end the 8635P reduces that to just 3.7GB/second per core.
Finally, how does all of this look with pricing taken into account?
As AMD’s more budget-friendly server platform, SP6 and Serano is fairly cheap as far as server chips go. In practice, almost all server builds are going to spend more on RAM to fill the server than they will the CPU itself. With the caveat that nearly no one pays AMD’s list prices for their server CPUs, AMD’s chip pricing is somewhat variable; lower SKUs are always cheaper, but they do not scale consistently with price. Which means the price-per-core bobs up and down from one SKU to the next.
The best value here is found in the 16 and 24 core SKUs, which at list price are under $50 per core. In relative figures, it is actually a pretty significant improvement over the other SKUs, which are $60+ per. Understandably, the 8 core SKU does not fare especially well here at $66 per core. Otherwise, the top-end 84 core SKU is actually decent for being a top chip, at $69 per core. The weakest SKU, interestingly enough, is the 64 core SKU, which is priced only a few hundred dollars less than the top-end chip, yet drops 20 cores in the process. As a result, it works out to being $86 per core – a significantly higher price than any of the other SKUs.
Final Words
As AMD’s more economical server platform, the EPYC 8005 Sorano family fills an important role in the company’s server lineup. With more than a few customers in need of a literally smaller chip family that can still bring the full advantage of the Zen 5 feature set but without quite so many CPU cores or expensive memory channels, the EPYC 8005 family fills that role well. And with AMD keeping the chip stack relatively simple at just 7 SKUs and without any major feature differentiators, it keeps the overall chip calculus for customers reasonably straightforward.
For pure compute throughput, the EPYC 8005 stack is rather clear-cut. The 8635P is easily the fastest chip in terms of total (on paper) compute throughput thanks to its 84 CPU cores, as well as looking very good in terms of power efficiency. The trade-off there is that clockspeeds are not all that high compared to other SKUs, and it has some of the highest contention for cache and memory resources. The smaller core count chips cannot push the same total throughput, but they can do have more cache and memory bandwidth available per core – and, depending on the specific SKU, often much higher clockspeeds as well. Overall, different SKUs excel in different metrics, so there is no one-size-fits-all recommendation across the entire stack, though the 32 core 8325P does tick a lot of boxes here as a potential jack-of-all-trades.
Still, all of this underscores the importance of understanding the workload that will be run on an EPYC 8005 server. Even with just 7 SKUs, the wide range in core counts (and fixed aspects elsewhere) means that optimizing for compute, for memory, and for cost all have different optimal point. For AMD it means the EPUC 8005 lineup can serve a wide breadth of customers, but it means customers need to do their homework to figure out just what they need.

articles.title: What is umami?
articles.text:
Characterised at the beginning of the 20th century in Japan, umami literally means “delicious taste” or “tasty taste”. Umami flavour was accepted as one of the five basic tastes at the beginning of the 2000s, on the basis of its detection by the taste receptors present within the patches of tissue or papillae on our tongue. Umami’s distinctive, savoury flavour is mainly produced by certain amino acids that make up proteins, including glutamic acid or its salt form, glutamate (sodium).
Umami has a unique characteristic: a phenomenon of synergy. This means that the flavour of glutamate is drastically increased by certain compounds found in certain foods or ingredients such as bonito – a cousin of tuna – dried (katsuobushi) or yeast extracts.
A mysterious flavour in the West
Although many molecules can produce the umami taste, it is one of the most little known and difficult sensations to describe, mainly because of the rarity of compounds that possess a pure umami taste.
The umami taste can however be generated among foods that are far more widespread than you would imagine: this is the case for algae (kombu algae), mushrooms (shiitake, truffle…) and also as has long been the case with basic kitchen staples like cheese (Parmesan, mature Comté, for example), cured meats (salami, dried ham…), fresh fish (especially bonito, salmon), seafood (shrimp, crabs, scallops…) or simply… tomato juice.
Glutamate is the reference molecule mainly behind umami, although it gets its salty taste from the presence of sodium ions. In powder form it tastes like cooking broth or soy sauce if you disregard its strong, salty flavour. In many Asian countries, glutamate (where its flavour is well known) is used in cooking as an ingredient in its own right.
Westerners on the other hand, lack a reference compound so tend to refer to a broth-like taste or borrow soy sauce as a familiar umami food which despite its strong saltiness, produces a pronounced umami taste.
The History of how umami was discovered
The discovery of umami is a long story. In his book la Physiologie du goût, published in 1826, French gastronome Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin describes a specific taste associated with the water-soluble part of meat. In 1866, German chemist Karl Heinrich Ritthausen found and chemically identified glutamic acid by breaking down wheat gluten and separating out a new compound, noting that it is capable of generating a different flavour.
The umami flavour concept was then put forward in 1908 by Kikunae Ikeda. A professor of chemistry at the time at the Tokyo Imperial University, Ikeda isolated glutamate from dried seaweed and was the first to describe its unique taste properties, which sit apart from the other basic tastes (sweet, bitter, sour and salty), and giving the flavour a Japanese name, in her “mother tongue”.
In 1913, Professor Shintaro Kodama highlighted the synergy (or the ability to amplify) of glutamate with compounds derived from RNA degradation (“ribonucleotides” such as inosinate and guanylate).
But it wasn’t until the 21st century that the umami flavour receptor called TAS1R1/TAS1R3 was identified in human papillae in 2002. From then onwards the umami flavour was completely accepted as the fifth basic taste among the scientific community.
The physiological role of umami
Our sense of taste is a chemical detection system dedicated to assessing food’s nutrient content. Its physiological role is to guide our food choices.
Therefore, detecting sweet molecules allows us to identify energy-rich nutrients, which is why we are naturally drawn to sweet things.
It’s a different story for the bitter taste, which provides the basis for our aversions to certain foods, allowing us to avoid potentially toxic compounds that have an unpleasant taste.
Detecting saltiness is of primary importance for maintaining our electrolyte balance. It is essential for finding sodium in our environment, because our bodies constantly lose sodium through our bodily excretory and secretory processes (sweat and urine).
Finally, acidity is an indicator of fruit maturity or the presence of microbial contamination. Identifying acidity also helps protect the body against eating food that is highly acidic that could damage our teeth and skin tissue.
But what about umami? It is believed that the physiological role of this particular taste is to detect amino acids and reveal the presence of protein and molecule-rich foods, which are crucial for ensuring our body functions properly.
Umami in world cuisine
Ingredients rich in umami compounds were introduced into our diet in ancient times to improve cooking. Garum was a condiment used in Rome as early as the Etruscan period. This sauce, derived from the fermentation of the heads and intestines of pickled fish, was used in many dishes and is comparable to nuoc-mâm, a Vietnamese sauce made from fermented fish in brine, that’s almost inseparable from spring rolls. We can also compare garum to pissalat, a French sauce made from fish (mackerel, sardines and anchovies) that is macerated in salt.
Soy sauce is a condiment hailing from China, which was introduced in Japan and spread worldwide. It is obtained by fermenting soya beans mixed with roasted cereals, and salt water. Its umami taste is very intense, as is its saltiness!
Another less well-known example to mention is Worcestershire sauce, which is popular in the UK. Invented in 1837, it is made from molasses and malt vinegar containing anchovies, onions and various spices. Viandox based on soy sauce, yeast extract, and meat extract, launched in France at the beginning of the 1920s, also packs a strong dose of umami.
And last but not least, if there is one cuisine that has showcased this taste, it is Japanese cooking culture. Unlike French cuisine, which is built on layering elements and tastes, it seeks to refine the plate by extracting the quintessence of its most prized produce such as fish, seafood, and seaweed.
Umami is one of the first flavours for babies’ mouths
Glutamate, i.e. the salt of glutamic acid, is commonly used as a flavour enhancer in the food industry in the form of monosodium glutamate (E621). The most widely consumed food additive, it has a global production estimated at several billion tons.
Although glutamate is the focus of debate over the risk of over-consuming it, it should be remembered that it is the most concentrated, free amino acid in breast milk, where it is present at a concentration of 175 milligrams per litre. Since this concentration sits above the threshold of what humans can detect (120 milligrams per litre), umami taste is one of the first flavours babies are exposed to.
Umami is lost on giant pandas
Umami’s physiological role is to alert carnivores to the presence of essential proteins. For example, physiological studies into cat food preferences have shown that our feline companions are also very fond of amino acids.
However, genetic studies have shown that the giant panda is insensitive to the umami taste. But what makes pandas (aguesiac or who have lost their sense of taste) unable to detect umami? The giant panda belongs to the ursid family, of the carnivore order. Their diet (bamboo represents 99% of what they eat) sets them apart from their other animal cousins as they are vegetarian, which paradoxically, makes them strict herbivores.
As mentioned above, umami compounds are detected in the mouth by a single receptor consisting of two subunits (TAS1R1 and TAS1R3). However, a study of the genetic heritage of the giant panda’s genetic heritage has shown that the gene encoding one of the subunits is defective, leading to an inactive umami-like receptor. It is for this reason that giant pandas have no perception whatsoever of umami. It is thought that, during evolution, this gene was lost, simply because the selection pressure on this receptor was let go of, as the species’ survival did not depend on its ability to identify protein.
This article is published as part of the Fête de la science, an annual event in France honouring Science in all its forms (which runs until October 12, 2026) – A The Conversation France partner event. articles.title: Vale do Silício cria escola gratuita que não dá diploma
articles.text:
A gestora de capital de risco Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) criou uma escola privada nos Estados Unidos para oferecer uma alternativa ao modelo tradicional de ensino superior. Batizada de Horowitz Andreessen Academy (HAA), a instituição pretende preparar estudantes para o mercado de tecnologia por meio de atividades práticas e do contato com empresários do setor, em um momento em que parte da indústria questiona a importância do diploma universitário.
A iniciativa tem o apoio de Marc Andreessen e Ben Horowitz, fundadores da gestora, que investe principalmente em startups e empresas de tecnologia com potencial de crescimento. O projeto recebeu US$ 42 milhões em investimentos, equivalentes a R$ 214,9 milhões. A primeira turma terá cerca de 50 alunos, com início previsto para setembro de 2027, e o programa será gratuito durante um ano.
Como vai funcionar a escola
A proposta da HAA é substituir parte das aulas predominantemente teóricas por projetos independentes voltados aos negócios. Segundo Gagan Biyani, CEO da instituição, o formato busca se aproximar do sistema tutorial da Universidade de Oxford e do método Montessori, em vez de seguir a estrutura de uma universidade convencional.
Os estudantes também terão acesso a palestras com executivos e empresários do setor de tecnologia. Entre os nomes citados pela academia estão Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia; Satya Nadella, CEO da Microsoft; e Travis Kalanick, cofundador da Uber.
Em uma publicação na rede social X, Biyani afirmou que a instituição pretende se tornar uma escola de elite, capaz de atrair talentos e prepará-los para o futuro. A declaração está alinhada à proposta de oferecer uma formação diferente daquela encontrada nas universidades tradicionais.
Instituição não terá diploma nem credenciamento
Apesar da proposta de formação, a academia apresenta limitações importantes em relação ao ensino superior convencional. Segundo a revista Fortune, a HAA não terá credenciamento oficial nem concederá diplomas. A instituição também não aceitará auxílio estudantil do governo federal dos Estados Unidos e não oferecerá garantia de emprego ou estágio remunerado.
A iniciativa acompanha um debate presente no Vale do Silício sobre a necessidade de concluir uma graduação para construir uma carreira de sucesso na tecnologia. Entre os exemplos frequentemente citados estão Bill Gates, cofundador da Microsoft; Mark Zuckerberg, cofundador do Facebook; e Steve Jobs, cofundador da Apple. Os três deixaram a faculdade antes de se formar.
Versão paga pode chegar em 2028
As inscrições para a primeira turma já estão abertas. O programa inicial será gratuito, terá duração de um ano e começará em setembro de 2027, com aproximadamente 50 estudantes.
Para 2028, a HAA planeja lançar uma versão paga de dois anos, caso obtenha a aprovação dos órgãos reguladores. De acordo com Biyani, as mensalidades deverão ser comparáveis às cobradas por universidades privadas de elite dos Estados Unidos.
A proposta amplia as opções de formação voltadas ao setor de tecnologia, mas não equivale a um curso universitário credenciado. O modelo da academia se concentra em projetos práticos e na aproximação com profissionais da indústria, sem oferecer um diploma ao final do programa.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: On peut désormais ranger ses canettes dans un Creeper de Minecraft
articles.text:
Si vous trouviez déjà les mini-frigos Xbox ou Astro Bot un peu bizarres, ceux-là devraient vous faire sourire. Ukonic propose un modèle Halo avec le casque de Master Chief en relief, un distributeur miniature façon Fallout et un Creeper de Minecraft. Ce dernier mesure tout de même 64 cm de haut, avec une tête et un corps qui s’ouvrent pour accueillir vos canettes.
Les trois sont en précommande chez Micromania, pour une sortie annoncée le 16 octobre 2026. Les prix varient selon la licence et la capacité :
- Le mini-frigo Minecraft de 8 litres est à 89,99 € chez Micromania
- Le mini-frigo Fallout de 7 litres est à 89,99 € chez Micromania
- Le mini-frigo Halo Master Chief 3D de 4 litres est à 79,99 € chez Micromania
Un Creeper de 64 cm, un Master Chief ou un distributeur Fallout
Chaque modèle reprend un élément emblématique de son jeu. Des trois modèles, celui de Minecraft est probablement le plus rigolo. Le Creeper donne littéralement sa forme à l’ensemble de l’appareil, jusqu’à ses quatre pieds. Haut de 64 cm, il s’ouvre sur deux compartiments, répartis entre la tête et le corps. L’intérieur et la base disposent même d’un éclairage vert. Ukonic annonce une capacité de 8 litres, permettant de ranger jusqu’à douze canettes de 355 ml.
Le modèle Halo met en avant Master Chief, le célèbre Spartan de la licence de Microsoft, avec un design en relief qui devrait attirer les regards sur un bureau ou à côté d’une console.
Quand au mini-frigo Fallout, il reprend l’allure plus sobre des distributeurs automatiques de la saga rétrofuturiste de Bethesda. Les trois modèles visent d’abord les collectionneurs.

articles.title: Honor Pad 20 Pro : cette nouvelle tablette perd déjà 100 € et arrive avec plusieurs cadeaux — Frandroid
articles.text:
Dernière arrivée dans la gamme d’Honor, la Pad 20 Pro se place sous la MagicPad 4, plus fine et plus haut de gamme. Elle reprend la diagonale de 12,1 pouces de la Pad 10, mais change de catégorie avec un Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 à la place du Snapdragon 7 Gen 3, et un écran à 165 Hz au lieu de 120 Hz. Honor la présente comme une tablette de travail, avec un Mode PC fenêtré censé remplacer un ordinateur portable d’appoint. Pour son lancement, elle perd 100 euros avec un code promo et plusieurs cadeaux sont à récupérer par la même occasion.
Les atouts de la Honor Pad 20 Pro
- Son écran 3K de 12,1 pouces rafraîchi à 165 Hz
- Une puce Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 et 256 Go de stockage
- Une batterie de 10 100 mAh rechargeable en 66 W
Le tarif officiel de la Honor Pad 20 Pro est de 599,99 euros. Le code AP20P fait tomber la note à 499,99 euros sur le site d’Honor, avec le clavier Smart Bluetooth et le stylet Magic-Pencil 4s offerts. Vous choisissez ensuite entre le casque Headphones Lite et le MiLi LiTag d’Honor Choice.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant la Honor Pad 20 Pro. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un grand écran 3K, mais en LCD
Honor a choisi un châssis monocoque en aluminium, avec un dos mat et un seul coloris gris. La tablette mesure 6,29 mm d’épaisseur. C’est fin, mais la MagicPad 4 descend à 4,8 mm, et l’écart se remarque quand on les compare. Sur la balance, elle pèse environ 537 g seule et monte à 800 g environ avec l’étui-clavier. Elle se glisse sans problème dans un sac à dos d’étudiant, sans pour autant battre des records de légèreté.
En façade, la dalle de 12,1 pouces affiche une définition de 3000 x 1872 pixels, soit 292 ppp, et occupe 88 % de la face avant. Honor annonce une fréquence de 165 Hz et une luminosité qui monte jusqu’à 700 nits. Bon, il s’agit d’une dalle LCD, donc sans les noirs profonds d’un OLED. C’est d’ailleurs l’un des deux points qui ont fait tiquer notre testeuse. Pour lire, annoter des PDF ou regarder une série, la définition reste confortable.
Un Mode PC pour remplacer l’ordinateur d’appoint
À l’intérieur, on trouve le Snapdragon 8s Gen 4 de Qualcomm, accompagné de 8 Go de RAM et de 256 Go de stockage. Le processeur a de quoi faire. Les 8 Go de mémoire vive sont plus justes pour une tablette qui doit jongler entre plusieurs fenêtres, et c’est le second point relevé dans notre test. Le logiciel tourne sous MagicOS 10.0, basé sur Android 16, et Honor promet six ans de mises à jour Android et de sécurité.
Le Mode PC est franchement le cœur du projet. La tablette gère le multitâche en fenêtres multiples ou en écran partagé, avec prise en charge de la souris, du clavier et du stylet. Le pack offert prend alors tout son sens, puisque sans clavier ce mode perd une bonne partie de son intérêt. Pour l’endurance, la batterie de 10 100 mAh se recharge en 66 W, et Honor annonce jusqu’à 12 heures de lecture vidéo. Ce chiffre reste à confronter à nos mesures.
Pour savoir comment elle s’en sort face à la MagicPad 4, lisez notre test de la Honor Pad 20 Pro, avec tous nos relevés sur l’écran, les performances et l’autonomie.
Si vous hésitez encore, notre comparatif des meilleures tablettes du moment rassemble les modèles que nous recommandons, toutes gammes de prix confondues.

articles.title: Star Citizen's single-player spin-off gets a Steam page, and early hands-on reports
articles.text:
Light at the end of the tunnel? After 14 years of development and over $1 billion in crowdfunding, Star Citizen remains in alpha with no final release date in sight. However, its single-player spinoff, Squadron 42, feels closer than ever. A new Steam page lists notably modest minimum system requirements, and streamers recently began sharing their hands-on impressions following a demo event.
Anyone who still believes in Wing Commander creator Chris Roberts' vision after 14 years of repeated delays can now wishlist Squadron 42 on Steam. The space simulation action game is a solo, story-based spinoff of Roberts' MMO, Star Citizen, which remains deep in development.
The Squadron 42 Steam page features a new trailer with a few gameplay snippets and lists the minimum system requirements. Many influencers and streamers were invited to play the game for around five hours on October 9 and 10, and have since shared their thoughts, offering more specifics on what players can expect when (if?) Squadron 42 goes public.
Earlier demonstrations showed a mix of on-foot first-person shooter action and flight-simulation combat with a heavy focus on immersion. Hands-on reports further explain that Squadron 42 isn't an open-world game, but rather a more linear experience that might feel unusual compared to other recent AAA games.
Previews also point out its heavily cinematic presentation. Recalling Wing Commander's FMV cutscenes, Squadron 42 features a star-studded cast including Gillian Anderson, Mark Hamill, Gary Oldman, Mark Strong, John Rhys-Davies, Liam Cunningham, Ben Mendelsohn, and Henry Cavill.
The recent updates also suggest the game might not be as demanding as this year's biggest releases. Although Squadron 42 requires Windows 11, CPU support extends all the way back to quad-core AMD Bulldozer and Intel Sandy Bridge chips from the early 2010s, such as the legendary i5-2500K.
Furthermore, the game requires DirectX 12 support but appears to support any DirectX 11.1-compatible GPU with at least 8GB of VRAM. PowerGPU founder Jese Martinez, who attended the preview event, claims he saw Squadron 42 average 180fps on an RTX 5090 in native 4K using the game's homegrown "StarAA" anti-aliasing solution. Still, the game requires 150GB of storage space.
Squadron 42 and Star Citizen have been in production on one level or another since 2011, which might explain the system requirements. Both have suffered repeated delays. While Star Citizen remains in alpha after $1 billion in crowdfunding, the solo spinoff has been content-complete since late 2025.
Roberts first targeted a 2026 launch in 2024 but recently used Grand Theft Auto VI's impending launch as an excuse for yet another delay. Squadron 42's Steam page now lists a second-quarter 2027 release window, and a more precise date might emerge soon.

articles.title: ChatGPT vs Claude : quel abonnement IA est le plus généreux ? Une étude a tranché
articles.text:
OpenAI a profité de sa conférence développeurs pour amputer ChatGPT Pro, son abonnement à 200 dollars par mois, de la moitié de ses capacités. À compter du 30 octobre, ses limites d’utilisation passeront de vingt à dix fois celles de la formule Plus, et le quota hebdomadaire de messages au modèle GPT-6 Pro de 200 à 100. Dans le même temps, une étude du cabinet SemiAnalysis conclut que les abonnements de Claude, son grand rival, en donnent beaucoup plus pour la même somme.
Un crédit pour faire passer la pilule, un palier Ultrafast au-dessus
Les abonnés conserveront leur tarif, mais pas leur confort. Outre les plafonds divisés par deux, OpenAI accompagne la transition d’un crédit de 2 500 dollars, de quoi amortir le changement pour les plus gros consommateurs. L’entreprise avait déjà suspendu les ventes de cette formule en septembre, ses serveurs ne suivant plus la demande.
Pour retrouver des limites larges, il faudra viser plus haut : un nouvel échelon à 500 euros mensuels met en avant des réponses accélérées. Fin septembre déjà, les tarifs des modèles GPT-6 facturés aux développeurs avaient été divisés par deux.
2,9 milliards de tokens contre un milliard
SemiAnalysis a retenu une méthode simple : mesurer ce que les abonnés consomment réellement, puis convertir cette consommation au prix des API, les interfaces facturées aux développeurs. Un abonné Claude engloutirait jusqu’à 2,9 milliards de tokens par mois, ces unités de texte que traitent les modèles, contre environ un milliard pour son homologue ChatGPT. Rapportée aux grilles tarifaires, la différence donnerait un rapport de un à cinq en faveur de l’offre d’Anthropic.
Le rapport de un à cinq doit toutefois beaucoup à la récente baisse des prix d’OpenAI. Des tokens moins chers côté API font mécaniquement fondre la valeur théorique attribuée à ChatGPT, sans que l’abonné y perde quoi que ce soit. D’autres mesures inversent d’ailleurs la hiérarchie, à l’image du coût par tâche accomplie, estimé à 0,72 dollar pour GPT-6.1 Sol contre 5,98 dollars pour Claude Opus. En juin, le même cabinet plaçait du reste l’offre d’OpenAI en tête de sa précédente comparaison.
L’étude livre aussi un chiffre côté Anthropic : ses abonnements accapareraient 42 % de la puissance de calcul dédiée au fonctionnement de ses modèles, pour environ 10 % de ses revenus.

articles.title: Fuite de données : la Cnaf suspend un site d'urgence après un « incident de cybersécurité »
articles.text:
Une nouvelle fuite de données frappe les services publics français. Ce samedi 10 octobre, la Caisse nationale des allocations familiales (Cnaf) a confirmé un incident de cybersécurité sur Vacaf, la plateforme d’aide aux vacances des Caf. Dans son communiqué, l’organisme indique qu’une fuite concernant les données des bénéficiaires a été signalée « hier soir ». Par précaution, l’accès au site vacaf.org a été rapidement coupé pour éviter toute nouvelle violation d’informations. La plateforme Vacaf permet aux familles éligibles de financer des séjours ou des colonies de vacances pour leurs enfants. Hébergée par un prestataire externe, la plateforme est pilotée par la Caf de l’Hérault.
À lire aussi : Fuite de données – le plus grand CHU de France (et d’Europe) a été piraté
Plus d’un million de dossiers piratés ?
Selon les premières analyses réalisées par la Cnaf, les données bancaires et les mots de passe d’accès aux services en ligne des Caf n’ont pas été compromis. Cependant, la Cnaf ne détaille pas les données touchées. Une plainte doit être déposée « dans les prochaines heures », et l’ANSSI ainsi que la CNIL ont été informées de la situation. Bonne nouvelle, les prestations des allocataires continuent d’être versées normalement. Le système Vacaf est totalement séparé du système qui gère les versements. Les séjours déjà réservés sont maintenus, mais les nouvelles réservations sont suspendues jusqu’à nouvel ordre. Les personnes concernées seront informées individuellement dans les plus brefs délais. En attendant, méfiez-vous des faux SMS et des faux e-mails qui prétendraient venir de la Caf.
« Dans l’attente des conclusions définitives des investigations, la Cnaf appelle chacun à la vigilance face à d’éventuelles tentatives d’escroquerie, d’hameçonnage ou d’usurpation d’identité qui pourraient exploiter le contexte de cet incident », explique le communiqué.
La Cnaf n’évoque pas le nombre de personnes concernées. Selon le site spécialisé FrenchBreaches, un pirate affirme détenir 1 191 967 dossiers d’allocataires. Quoi qu’il en soit, ce n’est pas la première fois que la Caf se retrouve dans le viseur des pirates. En décembre dernier, l’organisme avait déjà confirmé une fuite de données. Quelques mois plus tard, les données de bénéficiaires du RSA ont été piratées par le biais d’un service de l’État. L’incident vient s’ajouter à la longue liste de fuites enregistrées par les services publics français. Parmi les victimes, on trouve les impôts, l’ANTS ou encore France Travail, qui enquête d’ailleurs sur une nouvelle violation.

articles.title: Aquaponey et IA : des vérités peu glorieuses sur l'Internet
articles.text:
L'Étrange histoire de l'Aquaponey : mais de quoi est-il question dans ce livre au titre mystérieux ?
Comment les algorithmes nous bouffent le cerveau
J'ai lu L’Étrange histoire de l’Aquaponey, livre au titre si bizarre qu'il m'a fallu savoir de quoi il était réellement question. Alors non, les chevaux de petite taille n'y sont pas pour grand-chose. Voici plutôt ce que vous réserve cette lecture atypique.
L’Étrange histoire de l’Aquaponey est un ouvrage 100 % généré par un humain. Est-il vraiment nécessaire de le préciser ? Quand on le referme, c'est tout sauf un détail. Plutôt que de poneys, il y est surtout question d’intelligence artificielle générative, de bots, de faux avis et autres joyeusetés qui pullulent sur Internet. S'il ne s'adresse pas forcément aux internautes occasionnels, il retiendra assurément l'attention de ceux qui passent beaucoup de temps en ligne, ou dont le métier exige une utilisation intensive du web.
Sur fond de vers tirés de l'album Ok Computer du groupe Radiohead, dont les rimes accompagnent le lecteur au fil des chapitres, l'autrice Romane Maltnoy (avec les préfaces de Maltnoy Sylvain Montmory et Alan CladX) parsème ses pages de QR codes renvoyant vers des vidéos et titres musicaux. Mais ce sont surtout les faits et les chiffres égrenés au fil des pages qui font tout le sel de ce livre.
Bots hors de contrôle et vache folle : l'IA face à elle-même
En tant que journaliste, je connaissais déjà l'envers du décor et la façon dont une partie des contenus du web est altérée par des acteurs automatisés. Pourtant, cet ouvrage m'a permis de prendre véritablement conscience de l'ampleur du phénomène.
On y apprend par exemple que les bots, ces logiciels qui naviguent automatiquement sur Internet, étaient déjà majoritaires en 2025. Plus de la moitié de l'activité en ligne était donc d'origine non humaine à cette date, et il est fort probable que cette proportion ait encore augmenté aujourd'hui. Et nous ne parlons pas ici des “gentils robots” qui indexent les pages pour les moteurs de recherche, mais bien de ceux qui truquent le trafic à des fins trompeuses.
L'intelligence artificielle en prend aussi pour son grade. Dressant un parallèle audacieux avec la crise de la vache folle (épidémie qui infectait les consommateurs de bêtes nourries elles-mêmes avec des farines issues de leurs propres carcasses, beurk…), l'autrice évoque un “cannibalisme algorithmique”. Elle explique que les IA génératives se nourrissent parfois de leur propre production, multipliant ainsi les erreurs et ces fameuses hallucinations.
Faux contenus et réseaux sociaux : le danger pour les moteurs de recherche
Pour les éditeurs de sites web comme Les Numériques, qui s'efforcent de produire un contenu pertinent, notamment avec des tests de produits réalisés par des humains, l'arrivée de l'IA dans les réponses des moteurs de recherche pourrait poser un sérieux problème. Pas seulement pour notre modèle économique, mais aussi, à plus long terme, pour l'ensemble des internautes.
L’Étrange histoire de l’Aquaponey cite une étude du Pew Research Center indiquant qu'à peine 1 % des utilisateurs clique sur les liens au sein d'une réponse générée par l'IA dans Google. Vous avez d'ailleurs probablement déjà vu ce type d'encart s'afficher suite à une requête. En effet, pourquoi aller chez nos confrères de Marmiton piocher dans des dizaines de recettes de gâteaux au chocolat quand une IA nous servira directement la prétendue “meilleure” recette (spoiler : non) ?
Une mort annoncée pour tous les sites web qui vivent des visites et des contributions des internautes. Mais, dès lors, qui alimentera le contenu recraché par les IA si les humains ne sont plus en mesure de le faire financièrement ?
Il est également question des réseaux sociaux, et les révélations de cet ouvrage feront que vous ne regarderez plus jamais un post Facebook, Twitter ou LinkedIn de la même façon. Même punition pour les avis publiés par de prétendus “acheteurs” sur Amazon et consorts. Une excellente façon d'ouvrir les yeux, ou de refuser de les fermer face à un phénomène dont nous soupçonnions tous l'existence.
Un twist de fin façon roman et une révélation inattendue
Ceci n'est qu'un aperçu. Je vous laisse découvrir le reste de ce livre riche en passages qui visent autant son autrice que les lecteurs. On y trouve notamment des mots teintés d'ironie sur ces fameux prompts géniaux que nous utilisons tous, persuadés de faire mieux que le voisin (oui, bien évidemment, nous sommes tous exceptionnellement calés en prompts…). Bref, tout le monde a sa part d'ombre, des grands médias au très intrusif Google Discover, en passant par les créateurs de contenus.
Pour terminer, revenons-en à nos poneys. S'il est question de la discipline de l'aquaponey citée dans le titre, c'est parce qu'une manipulation a réussi à faire croire aux moteurs de recherche (et aux IA qui l'ont intégrée) que ce sport absurde allait figurer aux JO de Paris. Mais ce n'est pas la seule surprise de l'ouvrage. Construit à la façon d'un roman, il réserve un twist en fin de lecture qui nous livre des révélations inattendues sur l'autrice.

articles.title: Claude found 29,000 possible bugs in open source. Only 516 have been fixed.
articles.text:
Claude found 29,000 possible bugs in open source. Only 516 have been fixed.
Anthropic’s new OSS Scanner, launched last week as part of its broader Cyber Mission, exposes a problem inside the company’s security research operation. Claude is finding potential vulnerabilities faster than human researchers can verify them.
Over six months of scanning some of the world’s most widely used open source projects, Anthropic’s models surfaced more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities. Its human review pipeline, which relies on six external security research firms to reproduce and triage findings, has worked through only about 6,000.
A disclosure dashboard puts some numbers behind the problem. As of October 2, outside security firms had confirmed 5,674 of the 6,123 findings they reviewed as valid, but only 516 vulnerabilities had been patched upstream.
The company sent 6,157 findings to maintainers, and 584 CVE and GitHub Security Advisory identifiers were issued, though some findings received both. Roughly 23,000 candidates remain unreviewed.
Claude is finding potential vulnerabilities faster than human researchers can verify them.
How the fast track works
Instead of making maintainers wait for its researchers to work through the backlog, Anthropic is giving eligible projects free, periodic scans powered by its top models, including Claude Mythos. The findings go directly to maintainers, without anyone at Anthropic validating them first.
Anthropic says projects that received its first reports increasingly asked for everything else it had, and it has already sent nearly 5,000 unvalidated reports to maintainers who requested them. The company now calls the arrangement an “optional fast-track.”
Bypassing the backlog
Expert penetration testers who vet its coordinated disclosures were asked to check 97 critical and high-severity findings that an early version of the scanner produced across 48 projects. Eighty-five cleared the bar for disclosure, while 11 of the remaining 12 were real bugs that duplicated known issues or other findings from the scan. Only one was a false positive.
Those figures describe the scanner’s early output, but not the 29,000 candidates from Anthropic’s separate disclosure program. The sample says little about lower-severity findings or how the scanner will perform at scale. In its technical announcement, Anthropic acknowledged that maintainers have reported inflated severity ratings and cases where the scanner misunderstood a project’s threat model.
What maintainers are reporting
What separates these reports from a SAST alert queue is how they are packaged. Anthropic says reports include a self-contained reproducer, an explanation that, when possible, identifies where the bug was introduced through bisection, and a candidate patch when the model can produce one. Anton Arapov, director of OpenSSL Corporation, said the reports Anthropic sent, raw model output included, matched and sometimes beat what the project gets from human researchers. He added that a report with a working exploit attached is “basically job done for an engineer as you can verify it right away.”
Todd Ouska, founder of wolfSSL, reported that 72 of the 74 reports his team received were valid and five became CVEs. PostgreSQL committer Noah Misch said several reports arrived with fixes the project could use “nearly as-is.” Misch also credited fast-track access with letting PostgreSQL address the newest issues before they shipped in a GA release.
But the most pointed endorsement came from The cURL Project founder Daniel Stenberg, who spent last year publicly complaining about the flood of AI-generated slop hitting his project’s bug bounty, which curl shut down in January. He now says OSS Scanner found multiple issues in curl, including one of the worst vulnerabilities the project has seen reported in the last few years.
Anthropic builds each project in an isolated VM and cuts off internet access before scanning begins. Reports go directly to maintainers by email, and they can pause or opt out at any time. The GitHub repository contains the enrollment and configuration tools, but not the scanner itself.
Finding bugs versus fixing them
A reproducer and a proposed patch can save time, but maintainers still have to test the fix, handle backports, and ship it, sometimes knowing the change will break behavior users rely on, which is the tradeoff OpenSSH’s maintainers made when they deliberately broke two features in the name of security.
Anthropic is restricting access to established open source projects that have the resources to handle more vulnerability reports.
Anthropic is restricting access to established open-source projects with the resources to handle more vulnerability reports. Projects must meet OSS-Fuzz-style eligibility criteria, and Anthropic checks that the person signing up is a core maintainer. The company also expects participating projects to be keeping up with the high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities already reported to them.
Who gets OSS Scanner access?
The service targets projects equipped to handle that work. Eligibility follows OSS-Fuzz-style criteria for widely used, security-critical open source software. Anthropic verifies that applicants are core maintainers, and its FAQ says participating projects should already be keeping up with verified high- and critical-severity reports.
The disclosure terms give participating maintainers room to work at their own pace. Unvalidated scanner findings carry no 90-day clock. However, a report the company later validates through its standard program can be disclosed 90 days after maintainers learn a human has confirmed it.
Anthropic says it may eventually attach a disclosure period to some high-severity scanner findings after giving projects notice and a chance to opt out.
Eligible maintainers can get free Claude Max 20x subscriptions through Claude for OSS. The idea is to help projects keep up with the growing number of findings, but free access to Claude doesn’t give maintainers more time to review and ship fixes. And as other AI-assisted coding efforts have shown, code that compiles cleanly can still contain problems that human reviewers need to catch.

articles.title: Nachteulen im 9-to-5-Job: Warum starre Arbeitszeiten krank machen
articles.text:
Studie belegt: Warum Nachteulen im 9-to-5-Job früher krank werden
Menschen mit einer späten inneren Uhr haben ein um rund 70 Prozent höheres Risiko, vorzeitig aus dem Erwerbsleben auszuscheiden. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt ein Team von Forscher:innen der finnischen Universität Oulu, wie in einer im Fachjournal Occupational and Environmental Medicine veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist.
Die Mediziner:innen analysierten die Daten von 5.679 Teilnehmer:innen einer finnischen Geburtskohorte aus dem Jahr 1966. Die Beobachtung erstreckte sich über einen Zeitraum von zwölf Jahren, in dem das Lebensalter der Personen von 46 auf 57 Jahre anstieg.
Dabei zeigte sich, dass sogenannte Nachteulen deutlich häufiger eine Erwerbsminderungsrente in Anspruch nehmen mussten als Morgentypen (Lerchen) oder keine den beiden Extremen zuzuordnende Personen. Dieser Unterschied blieb bei beiden Geschlechtern als konstante statistische Größe bestehen, selbst als externe Faktoren wie Bildungsebene, Einkommen und der spezifische Beruf herausgerechnet wurden.
Wenn die innere Uhr gegen den Wecker arbeitet
Die Zuordnung zu den jeweiligen Biorhythmen erfolgte nicht allein auf Basis subjektiver Einschätzungen der Proband:innen. Das Team der Universität Oulu nutzte validierte Fragebögen, die detailliert erfassten, wie schwer das Aufwachen fiel und wie stark die Müdigkeit in der ersten halben Stunde des Tages ausgeprägt war.
Zusätzlich glichen die Wissenschaftler:innen diese Selbsteinschätzungen mit genetischen Daten aus einer früheren Erhebung ab. Dieser polygene Score für frühes Aufstehen bestätigte die biologische Basis der Angaben, wodurch eine Verfälschung der Ergebnisse durch rein persönliche Vorlieben unwahrscheinlich wurde.
Etwa 10 Prozent der befragten Männer und 12 Prozent der Frauen fielen am Ende der Auswertung in die Kategorie der Nachteulen. Die Gruppen der Morgen- und Zwischentypen machten jeweils mehr als 40 Prozent der Gesamtmenge aus.
Wie der soziale Jetlag Nachteulen unter Druck setzt
Die Auswertung ergab, dass fast die Hälfte der männlichen und gut 43 Prozent der weiblichen Nachteulen ihre allgemeine Gesundheit als schlecht einstuften. Sie berichteten häufiger über Schlaflosigkeit, geringere körperliche Aktivität und einen ausgeprägten sozialen Jetlag.
Dieser Jetlag entsteht, wenn die biologisch präferierte Schlafzeit klar von den tatsächlichen Zeiten an Arbeitstagen abweicht. Laut der ergänzenden Zusammenfassung auf StudyFinds führt diese Diskrepanz langfristig zu chronischem Schlafmangel, der kognitive Fähigkeiten beeinträchtigt und den körperlichen Abbau beschleunigt.
Erst als die Forscher:innen eben jene gesundheitlichen Einschränkungen und die absolvierten Arbeitszeiten in ihre Modelle einbezogen, schrumpfte die statistische Lücke zwischen Eulen und Lerchen messbar. Vor allem die geleisteten Wochenstunden und das Arbeiten in Schichten hatten einen starken Einfluss auf die Wahrscheinlichkeit eines frühen Berufsausstiegs.
Die medizinischen Folgen starrer Arbeitszeiten
Während über 70 Prozent der Nachteulen angaben, in regulären Tagesjobs zu arbeiten, war der Anteil an Nachtschichten bei ihnen dennoch signifikant höher als bei den Lerchen. Die Forscher:innen betonen, dass ein typischer Arbeitstag in Finnland um acht Uhr morgens beginnt, was einer Zeit entspricht, in der späte Chronotypen noch unterhalb ihres maximalen Leistungsniveaus operieren.
Die Daten offenbarten zudem weitere soziodemografische Auffälligkeiten innerhalb der untersuchten Gruppen. Nachteulen waren zwar im Durchschnitt höher gebildet, lebten aber seltener in einer Ehe oder festen Partnerschaft und waren häufiger von Erwerbslosigkeit betroffen.
Eine Erwerbsminderungsrente wird in dem untersuchten finnischen System nur bewilligt, wenn ein medizinisches Gutachten eine dauerhafte und schwerwiegende Einschränkung der Arbeitsfähigkeit bestätigt. Das bedeutet, dass der beobachtete Ausstieg nicht auf eine fehlende Motivation zurückzuführen ist, sondern auf nachweisbare medizinische Diagnosen fußt.
Die Studienautor:innen weisen explizit darauf hin, dass dieser Verlust von erfahrenen Arbeitskräften ein ernst zu nehmendes Problem für die Volkswirtschaften darstellt. Der unfreiwillige Abschied aus dem Berufsleben geschieht während der produktivsten Kernjahre einer normalen Karriere.
Trotz der umfassenden Datenlage weisen die Forscher:innen auf gewisse Limitierungen ihrer Methodik hin. So basierte die Erfassung des Chronotyps lediglich auf einer einmaligen Befragung im Alter von 46 Jahren, weshalb sich die Resultate vornehmlich auf diese spezifische Altersgruppe beziehen.
Das unbedingte Festhalten an konventionellen Arbeitszeiten, die sich vorwiegend am Rhythmus von Lerchen orientieren, benachteiligt die Gruppe der Eulen demzufolge systematisch. Ob asynchrone Arbeitsmodelle diese Entwicklung stoppen können, müssen weitere Analysen klären, da die Studie lediglich Beobachtungen festhält, aber keine Kausalität zwischen flexiblen Arbeitszeiten und einer sinkenden Rentenquote isolieren konnte.

articles.title: « Les usines se battent contre des usines » : c’est quoi ArsenalOS, le logiciel d’Anduril qui doit piloter la production d’armes américaines
articles.text:
Costard bleu, cravate rouge et casquette « USA » vissée sur la tête, le président américain Donald Trump a présenté, ce mardi 6 octobre, Arsenal-2, un chantier naval situé à Sparrows Point, près de Baltimore.
Destiné à fabriquer des composants des sous-marins d’attaque de classe Virginia, le site sera construit par Anduril. L’entreprise américaine de défense y engage 3,7 milliards de dollars de capitaux privés, auxquels s’ajoute un contrat de la Navy pouvant atteindre 2,9 milliards de dollars, dont les paiements dépendront des résultats de production.
Dans le communiqué qui accompagne cette annonce, Anduril décrit ce site comme un chantier « software-defined », comprenez organisé autour du logiciel. L’entreprise y met surtout en avant l’outil qui doit le faire fonctionner. ArsenalOS, dévoilé en juin dernier sur son blog, se veut la colonne vertébrale numérique de toutes ses usines.
Un seul système, du plan à l’atelier
« Parcourez les ateliers de nombreuses usines de défense et vous trouverez le matériel le plus avancé au monde suivi de la manière la plus archaïque qui soit », c’est en partant de cette affirmation qu’Anduril promeut ArsenalOS.
Malgré le « OS » de son nom, ArsenalOS est une plateforme qui relie entre eux les logiciels de production d’Anduril.
ArsenalOS doit réunir dans un même environnement toute la chaîne, de la conception à la maintenance sur le terrain. Il combine, selon Anduril, une plateforme maison baptisée Forge et des logiciels commerciaux tiers.
Quand un plan est modifié, le logiciel doit répercuter automatiquement le changement dans les instructions de travail, qu’il génère lui-même. Il garde la trace de la version utilisée pour chaque unité, ce qui permet de repérer les exemplaires à modifier. Il empêche en outre l’atelier de travailler sur un plan périmé.
Il vérifie aussi les stocks, guide les techniciens avec des instructions numériques et enregistre chaque soudure ou boulon serré, avec l’auteur et l’heure de l’opération.
Anduril compare ce processus à la « kill chain » militaire, qui va de la détection d’une cible à la frappe. Sa « build chain » va de la définition d’un besoin au déploiement, avec une différence revendiquée, puisqu’elle doit pouvoir rester ouverte aux modifications tant que le terrain l’exige.
Une promesse encore à démontrer
Anduril justifie ce projet par sa vision de la guerre moderne. « Les usines se battent contre des usines, à des centaines de kilomètres derrière les lignes de front », écrit l’entreprise, qui ajoute que les stocks d’armes déterminent désormais la dissuasion. L’entreprise promet des milliards de dollars d’économies et un modèle capable de s’adapter rapidement aux changements de commandes ou de fournisseurs.
Ces affirmations restent pour l’instant celles de l’industriel, qui reconnaît lui-même qu’ArsenalOS n’en est encore qu’à ses débuts. Anduril le présente aussi comme le socle d’Arsenal-1, une première usine installée près de Columbus, dans l’Ohio, où l’entreprise produit son drone de combat YFQ-44 Fury.
Ses communications ne détaillent pas non plus comment est protégé le système qui centralise, du plan initial jusqu’à la maintenance sur le terrain, l’ensemble des données de production d’armements.
Le chantier de Baltimore ne produira pas avant 2030, et c’est la Navy qui, par le biais du contrat indexé sur les résultats, dira si la promesse d’un chantier naval piloté comme un logiciel tient sur la durée.
